description: We are ITSTEP Odesa OrbitX, we are developing a calendar project with challenge name "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots"
summary:
We built FireSync, a web application designed to track and analyze active fire hotspots around the world. Our goal was to take decades of scattered satellite data and turn it into a clean, eas-to-use tool. The platform combines a full-screen interactive map with a burning activity calendar, sensor filters for both MODIS and VIIRS, intensity sliders for Fire Radiative Power, and analytical charts covering monthly trends, anomalies, and land cover breakdowns, plus quick CSV data exports.
One of the biggest problems in monitoring wildfires is that older MODIS records  and newer, higher-resolution VIIRS observations use different scales and cannot be compared directly. FireSync solves this by harmonizing these two datasets into a single, consistent timeline. Instead of jumping between disconnected databases, users can pick any region and immediately see how current fire activity compares to historical baselines over the last twenty-plus years.
With extreme fire weather becoming more common, responders, scientists, and land managers cannot afford to waste time sorting through fragmented raw files. FireSync turns complex NASA satellite feeds into clear, practical insights—helping teams spot unusual burning patterns early, measure the actual intensity of fires, and make faster decisions when it matters most.
details:
Impact

As extreme fire weather becomes more frequent, emergency responders, land managers, and researchers need fast, reliable situational awareness. FireSync turns decades of fragmented satellite records into an actionable burning activity calendar-helping teams anticipate peak fire windows, spot unusual seasonal anomalies early, and export clean CSV data in seconds to protect ecosystems and local communities.

Creativity

Instead of burying users in dense spreadsheets or static scientific charts, we built FireSync as an interactive, dark-mode mission control center. Pairing a heat-coded calendar directly with a full-screen global map lets users see the rhythm of seasonal burning at a glance, while tucking hotspot telemetry popovers and deep analytics into clean on-demand modules keeps the interface fast and uncluttered.

Validity

Our platform is grounded in real Earth Observation science and built for practical usability. Because VIIRS detects smaller fires than legacy MODIS sensors, merging raw counts creates false spikes; we solved this by normalizing detections into grid cells, separating sensor toggles, and adding Fire Radiative Power intensity filters alongside confidence metrics so users can distinguish major wildfires from routine agricultural burns.

Relevance

FireSync relies directly on NASA’s open Earth Observation datasets-specifically over twenty years of MODIS and VIIRS active fire records starting from November 2000. Without NASA’s continuous satellite monitoring and harmonized thermal anomaly archives, building a unified multi-decade timeline to compare current burning activity against historical baselines would not be possible.

Tools & Tech Stack

We designed and prototyped the entire user interface, interactive components, and dark-mode GIS visual system in Figma. For the frontend, we built the web application using Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS to handle responsive state management and styling, integrated Leaflet to render the interactive global hotspot map, and used MkDocs to organize clean project documentation. On the backend, we powered our API and data harmonization pipeline with Python 3.11, FastAPI, and NumPy to process and normalize NASA's historical MODIS and VIIRS records, storing the structured time-series grid data in SQLite. Finally, our team wrote, debugged, and tested the entire codebase using Visual Studio Code and PyCharm.
